# Energy-Based Models {#sec-energy-models}

## From energy to probability

An **energy-based model (EBM)** associates to each configuration $x$ a scalar
*energy* $E_\theta(x)$ and defines a Gibbs distribution

$$
p_\theta(x) = \frac{1}{Z(\theta)}\, e^{-E_\theta(x)},
\qquad
Z(\theta) = \sum_x e^{-E_\theta(x)} .
$$


Low-energy configurations are more probable. This is the Boltzmann distribution
derived in @sec-free-energy, at unit temperature and with a learnable energy
function in place of a physical one. EBMs are attractive because they impose no
normalization constraint on $E_\theta$ and can flexibly express dependencies.


## The challenge: the partition function

The difficulty is the partition function $Z(\theta)$, which is generally
intractable. Equivalently — and this is the more useful way to see it — the
quantity we cannot compute is the free energy $-\log Z$. Learning and inference
therefore rely on techniques such as:

- **Sampling** (MCMC, Langevin dynamics) to approximate expectations,
- **Score matching** and **contrastive** objectives that avoid computing $Z$
  [@hinton2002cd],
- **Variational** bounds, which are exactly the free-energy inequality
  $F(q) \ge F$ of @sec-free-energy applied to a tractable family of $q$
  [@lecun2006tutorial].

## Connection to this book

Energy-based modeling is the substrate on which later chapters build:

- *Maximum-entropy learning* (@sec-max-entropy) uses Gibbs distributions to
  derive game-theoretic valuations [@bian2022energybased].
- *Energy-based reasoning* (@sec-energy-reasoning) treats an energy landscape as
  an object to guide, refine, and search over at inference time.
